mayor councillors I'm here today to support the staff recommendation that council direct them
to create a new schedule under the city's business licensing bylaw 2009-18-885 to regulate
the licensing of short-term rental accommodations before council today. Online short-term rental
platforms have afforded homeowners an opportunity to make extra money by hosting guests for short
stays in their home and has been a disruptor in our hospitality industry since 2009 when
Airbnb launched in Canada. I'm grateful Guelph is set to regulate this business
model which is dependent upon the commodification of our homes. The fact
there is a housing crisis in Ontario has been predominant in the news including
here in Guelph and even in this chamber as is evidenced by the mayor's poverty
tax force. The 2001 census data shows Guelph has a population of almost 144,000.

The 2001 point in time by name list has approximately 250 of those Guelphites identified as experiencing homelessness on October 20th, 2021, including 40 individuals under the age 25, with half of those being minors under 16.
On February 16, 2023, Guelph Today reported that our city is the ninth most expensive city in all of Canada to rent a one-bedroom apartment.
And the staff report identified 169 unique short-term rental accommodation listings in Guelph on various online platforms.

Given this information, I was aghast when I heard Councillor Gibson seem to state that people who have commodified housing as their retirement planning tool would potentially suffer monetary loss if they couldn't have three or four or even five short-term rental properties in the city.

I find it incomprehensible that any elected official would seemingly ignore the major housing crisis where people are living in tents, in the bush, in sub-zero temperatures, to advocate for retirement plans.
Especially since there is no restriction on how many long-term rental properties any one individual can have.

After hearing that Councillor Gibson might entertain putting forward an amendment to increase the number of dedicated short-term rentals permitted under each license, I did some research on similar licensing bylaws in Ontario.
A quick Google search afforded me multiple municipalities of which I reviewed 14.
I chose some that I know are comparators for Guelph as well as some of my favourite cottage country areas.
every municipality I reviewed had a restriction on the number of short-term
rentals permitted per license every municipality had the requirement that the
licensee must have their primary residence as the licensed property many
municipalities are limited to primary residence only some allow a second
property some require the online platform to be licensed some have a
demerit system. A few have a limited number of days per year and a couple have a $5 million
insurance requirement. Attachment 5 in the report lists the comparator municipalities and was
available to councillors as well as the public in advance of committee of the whole, which leaves me
unsure why any councillor would postulate more than one additional property per licensee.

While I was confused by the somewhat different answers provided to Councillor Gawler and Mayor Guthrie when they each asked essentially the same question, I believe I have it correct that in the proposed schedule to be added to the City's business licensing bylaw, an individual licensee must have their primary residence as the location for a short-term rental, be it a room in their home, a basement unit, or an accessory dwelling.
and there's an opportunity for a second property that is a dedicated short-term rental accommodation.
As a few councillors have stated, I believe the proposed schedule strikes an appropriate balance
for our residents seeking long-term homes and for visitors wanting to stay in our beautiful city.
Today, I look forward to a unanimous vote of council on this Made in Guelph bylaw
to bring us in line with other municipalities regarding short-term rental accommodation.
